content: Over the last forty years, continuous electronic fetal monitoring (EFM) has been increasingly utilized during labor to detect fetal acidaemia. The goal of this monitoring is to prevent conditions such as hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, permanent neurological damage, and fetal death. While EFM is highly sensitive, it has a low specificity and a high rate of false positives. This high false positive rate has led to unnecessary operative interventions for many fetuses who were not actually at risk of neurological injury or death. Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) has been developed as a method to directly measure fetal cerebral oxygenation. The aim of this technology is to more accurately identify fetuses who are genuinely at risk of adverse outcomes. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of using near-infrared spectroscopy for fetal assessment during labor on both maternal and perinatal outcomes. A search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register in August 2009 to identify relevant studies. The selection criteria included randomized controlled trials that compared the use of near-infrared spectroscopy with continuous EFM alone or with continuous EFM combined with scalp pH measurement. No randomized controlled trials were identified during the search. If any trials had been found, both authors would have independently assessed their eligibility and quality. As no trials were identified, no studies were included in this review. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence to evaluate the effectiveness of fetal surveillance using near-infrared spectroscopy.
